clinical: Cirrhosis

Long-term liver damage, most often from alcohol, hepatitis B or C, or fatty liver disease, replaces normal liver tissue with scar and regenerative nodules. The scarring distorts the lobes and blocks blood flow through the liver.
Viral hepatitis
Viral hepatitis inflames the liver cells and can cause jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) and pain under the right ribs.
Caput medusae

In portal hypertension, the paraumbilical veins that run with the round ligament in the free edge of the falciform ligament can dilate. This creates a visible network of swollen veins around the navel.
Gallstones
Gallstones often lodge in the neck of the gallbladder (Hartmann's pouch) and can block the cystic duct, causing acute cholecystitis (an inflamed gallbladder).
Obstructive jaundice
A stone or tumour blocking the common bile duct stops bile reaching the duodenum. This causes obstructive jaundice, with yellow skin, pale stools and dark urine.
Acute pancreatitis
Inflammation of the pancreas, most often from gallstones or alcohol, activates digestive enzymes inside the gland itself. It causes severe upper abdominal pain that radiates through to the back.
Pancreatic head cancer
A tumour of the pancreatic head can squeeze the common bile duct, which runs in a groove on the back of the head. This blocks bile flow and causes painless jaundice.
Duodenal ulcer
Most duodenal ulcers form in the first part of the duodenum (D1). They are commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or regular NSAID use.
Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
The third part of the duodenum can be squeezed between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery, causing obstruction with vomiting.
Pyloric stenosis
In infants, the pyloric muscle thickens and narrows the stomach outlet, causing forceful, non-bilious vomiting a few weeks after birth.
Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease flattens the villi of the proximal small intestine (the duodenum and jejunum), so nutrients are absorbed poorly.
Portal hypertension

Increased resistance to blood flow through the liver, most often from cirrhosis, raises pressure in the hepatic portal vein. Blood is diverted into side channels, such as the veins of the lower oesophagus, which can swell into varices that bleed.
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Blockage of the hepatic veins stops blood leaving the liver, causing congestion, pain under the right ribs and ascites.
Bleeding duodenal ulcer
The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, so an ulcer eroding through the back wall can cause severe bleeding.
Cystic artery in gallbladder surgery
The cystic artery, usually a branch of the right hepatic artery, supplies the gallbladder. Surgeons must identify and control it during gallbladder removal (cholecystectomy).

parts.description: The right lobe is the largest part of the liver, filling the right upper abdomen beneath the right dome of the diaphragm. On the front it is separated from the smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, while its underside (the visceral surface) carries the gallbladder fossa, the groove for the inferior vena cava and impressions from the right colic flexure, right kidney, right suprarenal gland and duodenum. It contains most of the liver's mass, so it is the main part removed in a right hepatectomy.

The porta hepatis (hilum of the liver) is the transverse fissure, about 5 cm long, on the underside of the liver between the quadrate lobe in front and the caudate lobe behind. The hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery proper enter the fissure, and the right and left hepatic ducts leave it, together with lymphatics and nerves. From front to back the structures lie as ducts, artery, then portal vein, and the hepatoduodenal ligament (the free edge of the lesser omentum) attaches to its margins.

The bare area of the liver is a triangular patch on the back of the right lobe that has no peritoneal covering and lies directly against the diaphragm, attached by loose connective tissue. It is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament, which meet laterally at the right triangular ligament. Because it is not covered by peritoneum, a liver abscess here can track through the diaphragm into the pleural cavity.

The coronary ligament is a double sheet of peritoneum that runs from the diaphragm onto the back of the right lobe of the liver, enclosing the bare area between its two layers. The superior layer continues onto the right layer of the falciform ligament, while the inferior layer passes down onto the right kidney and suprarenal gland as the hepatorenal ligament. The two layers meet laterally at the right triangular ligament.

The right triangular ligament is the short lateral fold where the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament meet at the apex of the bare area. It attaches the right lobe to the diaphragm, and it is divided when the right lobe is mobilised at operation, such as before a right hepatectomy.

The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped double fold of peritoneum, a remnant of the embryonic ventral mesentery, that runs from the umbilicus and anterior abdominal wall up to the front and top of the liver and the diaphragm. It marks the division between the right and left lobes on the front of the liver. Its free lower edge holds the ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) and small paraumbilical veins, and above, its two layers split to join the coronary and left triangular ligaments.

The cystic duct is about 3 to 4 cm long and joins the neck of the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct, usually on its right side, to form the common bile duct. Its mucosa forms a spiral fold, the valve of Heister. With the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver, it bounds Calot's triangle, which contains the cystic artery. Clearing this triangle at cholecystectomy lets the surgeon identify the cystic duct and cystic artery before they are clipped.

Neck of the pancreas: the short, narrow part joining the head to the body, lying in front of the portal vein, which is formed behind it by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. The pylorus lies in front of it. Its posterior surface is grooved by the portal vein, and surgeons tunnel behind the neck along this plane during pancreaticoduodenectomy.

The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) runs from the tail through the body and neck, turns down through the head, and joins the bile duct at the major duodenal papilla. It receives smaller side branches along its course and carries alkaline, enzyme-rich pancreatic juice, about 1.5 litres a day, into the duodenum. Obstruction, from a stone, a tumour or chronic pancreatitis narrowing, raises pressure in the duct and can activate enzymes inside the gland, causing pancreatitis.

The descending (second) part of the duodenum is the downward limb of the C-shaped duodenal loop, about 7-10 cm long, lying to the right of L1 to L3 in front of the right kidney and wrapped around the pancreatic head. Its posteromedial wall carries the major duodenal papilla, where bile and pancreatic juice enter, with the minor papilla a little above it. Its mucosa has prominent circular folds, and the major papilla is the landmark used to reach the bile duct at endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

The pylorus is the narrow outlet at the lower end of the stomach, where the pyloric antrum narrows into the duodenum. It is guarded by the pyloric sphincter, a thick ring of circular smooth muscle that meters chyme (partly digested food) into the duodenum and prevents backflow into the stomach. It lies at the transpyloric plane (L1), a key surface landmark, and in infants its muscle can thicken, causing pyloric stenosis with projectile vomiting.

The jejunum is the middle part of the small intestine, running from the duodenojejunal flexure in the upper left abdomen to join the ileum. It is a major site for absorbing sugars, amino acids and fats, and it is recognised by its thick wall, tall, dense circular folds and long villi. Its mesenteric arteries form fewer arcades than those of the ileum, with longer straight branches.

The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium of the heart. It ascends on the right of the vertebral column, behind the head of the pancreas and the portal vein, and sits in a deep groove on the bare area of the liver, where the hepatic veins drain into it. It pierces the diaphragm's central tendon at T8, and it forms the posterior boundary of the omental (epiploic) foramen, the doorway into the lesser sac.

The abdominal aorta is the continuation of the thoracic aorta below the diaphragm, entering the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12. It descends on the left of the vertebral bodies, lying behind the pancreas, and divides at L4 into the two common iliac arteries. Its branches to the foregut and midgut are the coeliac trunk (T12) and superior mesenteric artery (L1). A localised swelling of its wall (aneurysm) is a common, dangerous condition in older people.

The left gastric artery is the smallest branch of the coeliac trunk. It runs up to the cardia, where the oesophagus enters the stomach, and then along the lesser curvature, giving small oesophageal branches. Its companion vein drains into the portal system, so in portal hypertension this route can enlarge into oesophageal varices.
